No defects found. The page is sound, self-contained (no external resources, no JS errors), and the claimed mechanism is fully corroborated.

Minor selector nuance (not a defect): the element-under-test selector uses :nth-of-type(2), which keys off element type (span) among siblings rather than the .pseudo-link class. It resolves correctly here because both spans are adjacent siblings in .card-actions and Print is the 2nd span, but a more robust selector would be .pseudo-link:nth-child(2) or an id.

Scenario/.md over-claims the AT behavior: it states 'AT does not expose them as real links' and 'absence of href makes the element a non-link in the accessibility tree', but the Chromium AX tree (inspect output backendNodeIds 22/24/26/29/31) exposes all five toolbar anchors with role:'link' and correct names (Reply/Reply all/Forward/Archive/Delete). The name/role aspect of the claim is inaccurate for this engine. This does NOT change the 2.1.1 verdict (which rests on keyboard unreachability), but the prose should be corrected to avoid an inaccurate AT claim.
Minor: the case overlaps in mechanism with the sibling F42-style cases in this folder (href-less <a onclick>); distinctness rests on the webmail framing/content rather than a novel mechanism.

Minor framing mismatch (not a defect): F42 is titled/scoped around emulating LINKS (role 'link'), and the .md quotes its 'emulated link' example, but the element under test uses role='button'. The SC 2.1.1 logic (focusable but not keyboard-activatable) and the cited Procedure check #2 apply identically to a button, so the citation still correctly supports the 2.1.1 mechanism — but a stricter reviewer could note the role mismatch with F42's link framing.

The mechanism leans on the legacy 'keypress' event (deprecated). It currently fires in Chromium so handleKey runs, but even if keypress did not fire, the room would still never open from the keyboard — so the 'failed' outcome is robust either way (noted for completeness, does not affect correctness).

Cosmetic-only: the CSS comment at line 24 says the kebab has 'onkeyup wired up', but the element and JS actually use onkeydown (kebabKey via onkeydown=). Doc/comment inconsistency, not a functional defect.
The .md also implicates 4.1.2 (aria-expanded never updates), which is true, but the page's primary/labeled SC is 2.1.1 and the failure is correctly a 2.1.1 keyboard-operability failure.

This is a PASS-boundary case by design: the documented 'issue' is deliberately a NON-defect. errorIsReal=false correctly reflects that no accessibility error exists; expectedOutcomeCorrect=true reflects that the documented 'passed' outcome is right. This is not a fault in the page — just noting the semantics of the flags for this case type.
Minor: the doc/page repeatedly self-assert 'Verified behaviourally (headless Chromium)'. I independently re-verified rather than trusting the assertion; the behavior matches, so no defect.

Minor authoring smell (not a 2.1.1 defect): the add-item label at line 51 uses both class="visually-hidden" and an inline style="position:absolute;left:-9999px". The .visually-hidden class is never defined in the <style> block; only the inline style actually hides it. Harmless but redundant/dead class reference.

Citation grep for an exact one-line match fails only because the quoted sentence wraps across source lines (51-53 in keyboard.html, 10-14 in F54.html); the text is verbatim once line-break whitespace is normalized, so this is NOT a citation defect.

Cosmetic, non-page issue: the inspect tool truncates two button accessible names in tabOrder (renders 'Move ... do' instead of 'Move ... down'). The page source aria-label (lines 55/63) and the AX tree both expose the full 'down' name, so this is a tool display artifact, not a defect in the page.

Minor citation-grep nuance (not a defect): the keyboard.html quote does not match a single-line grep because the source wraps it across three indented lines ('...do not require path dependent input.' splits with newlines+indentation between words). The text IS present verbatim modulo whitespace, which the task explicitly allows; the G202 (primary task citation) and F54 quotes both match character-for-character.

Minor semantic note (reinforces, does not weaken the verdict): the square uses role='application' on a div that is not focusable (no tabindex) and handles no keystrokes — application role signals AT to forward keys to the app, yet nothing consumes them, which is itself dubious authoring but does not change the 2.1.1 failure.

Minor citation hygiene: the .md doc's FIRST citation points to `wcag-understanding/keyboard.html`, which does not exist under refs/ (no WCAG Understanding HTML files are vendored). The authoritative (Trusted Tester) citation is fully correct: the quote 'PASS if BOTH true: 1. All functionality can be accessed and executed using the keyboard, AND 2. All essential information can be accessed via keyboard OR is available elsewhere on the page.' matches refs/trusted-tester/sc-2.1.1-keyboard.md lines 36-38 verbatim and directly supports the mechanism.

Minor citation nuance (not a defect): the headline verbatim quote (TT 4.A item 2a) is specifically about `title` attributes ('place keyboard focus; if the tooltip does not appear within two seconds...'), whereas this page uses a JS-built tooltip with no `title` attribute. The mechanism is nevertheless squarely covered by the broader essential-information provisions the doc ALSO cites verbatim (TT 4.A item 2c 'available elsewhere' + the Notes 'essential' definition), so the citation as a whole adequately supports the FAIL.

Self-imposed verification artifact only (no page defect): an initial cloneNode(true)+textContent check falsely suggested the caveat appeared outside the .tips payload; the authoritative innerText check disproved it — the caveat ('30 seconds', 'reclaim', 'lost', '12-month/committed-use') is in NONE of the visible page text, confirming 'disclosed nowhere else'.

Minor SC-framing nuance (not a defect): pure information-access via a title maps as naturally to 1.3.1/4.1.2/1.4.13 as to 2.1.1's 'functionality operable through keyboard' wording. The case is internally consistent because it explicitly relies on the Trusted Tester Test 4.A essential-information branch, which the cited reference (lines 24-34, 42) does scope to 'essential information provided by interactive elements' including tooltips — so the label is defensible under the named methodology, but a non-TT reviewer could file this under a different SC.

Could not execute axe-core directly (module not installed in eval scope); automated-detectability is established by reasoning rather than an axe run, but the conclusion (no axe/WAVE/Lighthouse rule flags essential prose trapped in a title on a non-focusable span) is high-confidence.

No defects found. This is a correctly-labeled PASS case, and the documented mechanism is sound. (A minor note, not a defect: the .md frames the case under 'why it does NOT fail' — a reviewer should read this as expected-outcome=passed, which it correctly states on lines 41/44.)
No defects found. The page is a faithful, self-contained reproduction of WCAG F55 with correct outcome label and accurate citations.

Minor nuance (not a defect): the .md claims static tools 'miss it' because it is behavioral. That is true of mainstream static checkers (axe-core/WAVE/Lighthouse) which analyze a DOM snapshot where the button is a valid named focusable native control with no missing/empty attribute. However a SPECIALIZED keyboard-focus-retention checker (e.g. one that dispatches focus and re-reads document.activeElement, exactly like this corpus's own probe) could automate detection. requiresHumanJudgment is still TRUE under the corpus criterion because the failure is NOT a lint-catchable static/markup defect (an onfocus attribute is not per se an error), but the case is closer to 'specialized-dynamic-tool-detectable' than to 'irreducibly human-semantic'.

Minor: the '...' in the Trusted-Tester quote elides the tail of clause 2 ('OR is available elsewhere on the page'); the stitched fragments are verbatim and adjacent (Evaluate Results items 1 and 2), so this is acceptable but not a contiguous single sentence.
No substantive defect found in the case. Citation, mechanism, and outcome all hold up.

Narrative inaccuracy (non-blocking): both the HTML comment (line 73) and the .md doc (line 20) claim the listbox uses aria-activedescendant, but the implementation actually uses roving DOM focus via opt.focus() (lines 116/127/128) and the options have no id and no aria-activedescendant attribute anywhere. This is a roving-tabindex-style listbox, not an activedescendant one. It does NOT change the verdict (and is in fact what makes the bug possible: real DOM focus moves to the option, firing the focus event); it is only a stray/incorrect descriptor in the prose.

Minor: the .md 'Why automated tools miss it' overstates that no static tool could catch it; a behavioral/dynamic AT-driven checker that arrows through options and re-reads activeElement after a macrotask could detect it. Still genuinely outside the reach of axe/WAVE/Lighthouse, so requiresHumanJudgment stands.

Minor (non-blocking, cosmetic): editor copy at HTML lines 70-72 says 'press Tab from the editor to the toolbar', but the toolbar precedes the editor in DOM/tab order (tabOrder stops 0-5 = buttons, stop 6 = editor; Puppeteer afterTab.tag=BODY), so the toolbar is reached via Shift+Tab from the editor. Narrative-only inaccuracy; no effect on the 2.1.1 verdict.
Note (not a defect): intentional PASS/true-negative boundary (md failure-mechanism: NONE); errorIsReal=false reflects that there is correctly no failure to find, and the 'passed' label is accurate.

Minor design nuance (not disqualifying): #map uses role="application" on a generic div with no exposed operable children, so the geolocation function is undiscoverable to AT beyond the visible help-text span. This compounds (rather than weakens) the 2.1.1 lockout, but a stricter reviewer could note the case also brushes a name/role/discoverability concern; the page is correctly scoped to the timing gate so it does not affect the 2.1.1 verdict.

Minor realism leak (not a verdict problem): the visible .note div (HTML lines 54-64) is a meta-explanation of 'why automated checkers pass this page', which a genuine production banking page would not contain. It does not affect the element under test or the SC outcome, but it telegraphs the answer and makes the page look like a corpus artifact rather than a natural sample.

The keystroke-dynamics gate is silent/runtime-only with no DOM artifact, so the issue is undetectable to static checkers by design (intended), but also means a reviewer cannot confirm it without dynamic typing — corroboration relies on reading the JS, not any browser signal.

None material. This is a PASS case and the documented mechanism is sound. Minor: the inspect tabOrder shows role:null for confirmBtn at the raw style layer, but the AX block correctly resolves role:button / name 'Confirm payment' (native button), so no actual naming/role defect.

Minor (not a defect): the discount code FORGE-FOUNDER-30 is hardcoded in the visible JS source (lines 99/123), and #apply accepts it untimed if typed (confirmed via sim: status='Founders' price applied: $59.00'). Realism note: a Date.now()-based 600ms window resets even on legitimate fast typists who pause mid-burst; this is the intended barrier but also means the gate is brittle — does not affect the SC verdict.

Minor (non-defect) note: the explanatory '.note' paragraph that reveals the trick (debounce/3-press) is rendered as visible body text and appears in the AX tree; this is unusual self-documentation but does not change the SC 2.1.1 verdict.
